utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, all. As you can see, the Bench is slightly reduced. I would say it's missing its most vital component. However, Judge Van Den Wyngaert and I have decided, invoking 15 Rule bis (A), to continue the hearing in the prospect that Judge Parker will be able to join us later in the day. May I remind the witness, sir, that the affirmation that you took at the beginning of your testimony is still applicable. And I believe we left it with you, Mr. Guy-Smith. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sir, how tall are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: 1.74 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you consider yourself to be a tall man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, average.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: An individual who was 180 metres, that individual would be a tall man; correct? 1.8 metres.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: He could be tall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say he could be tall, I take it that when you use the words "could be," in your estimation as somebody who you have to look up to as somebody who you consider to be a tall man, and I'm referring to the issue of someone who is tall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you first spoke with members of the OTP back in May, at that point in time, when you were speaking to them, you were trying to tell them the truth, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. But not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, when you say "not all of it," we'll get to that in a moment. At that point in time when you first spoke with these folks, you had learned that you were no longer a suspect and now were in the position of a witness. So you had nothing to be concerned about; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during the time that you were speaking with them in May, you discussed with them a series of subjects; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the things that you talked about were the guards at Lapusnik; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during that time you were asked questions about who the guards were at Lapusnik; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that regard while you were talking with them, you didn't hesitate to tell them that the guards were two individuals who you identified as Zenel and Timi; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. But not as guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During your first interview in May, you made it very clear that there was an individual present for a short period of time who had an injured leg; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That individual stayed in the kitchen for about ten days; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Correct. Not in the kitchen, near the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Near the kitchen. And that individual's name was Shala; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, also during that interview you were asked a series of questions about your involvement with an individual by the name of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, if would you take a look, I believe it's at the very -- close to the top of your page 16, and if you go down one, two, three -- I believe it's -- if you go down 12 lines, you will see the question asked. Do you see that? And by that I'm getting to the following question --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Was Shala one of the people who talked about this place being used to detain people?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, I can't find it on page 16. I can't find this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let's try it one more time. You'll see the following question. It says: "Okay. I will -- will concentrate on these three Serbs you are mentioning, but first I want you to answer the question. Was one Shala one of the people who talked about this thing towards the end of this period that you are mentioning?" And you answered: "No, because I didn't have contact with Shala."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you had your interview in May, your next interview was in the middle of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your interview in June, you once again discussed the issue of who were the guards at Lapusnik; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You identified the guards in Lapusnik as being Zenel and Timi. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't remember saying this. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With Mr. Younis's help, interview of June 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring you specifically to page 42. And I've done it in such a way if you want I can just give him that one section. Page 42, 43, 44. You have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you see the question asked: "Okay. Can you remember who were the guards at this place?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: On the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, I can't find it. I can't find this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might give him my -- I have it -- I have extracted those particulars, so let me give him mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Any objections to that, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could look at it first. Is it on page 42? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. June 17th transcript, page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The problem is for some reason this pagination is different from the one I have and the one I believe the witness has, which may explain why he couldn't find it on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It may well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But now I need to find where it is on our pagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is -- I received -- these are documents I received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: We understand that. There may be a need to calibrate and we're waiting for Mr. Whiting. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I've found it. It's only about a half page off. I found it. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: So I suggest we make sure what the witness now has what should be in front of him and then Mr. Guy-Smith can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Very good. It's -- on our version it's on page 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked the following question: "Can you remember who the guards were at this place?" Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You gave an answer. The answer you gave was: "The guards were changed." True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, before I go any further with regard to what you -- what you said in your interview of June 17th, when you were giving statements on June 17th, at that time you certainly were telling the truth, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I believe, yes. I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Unlike before in May when you sometimes told the truth. By the time we reached June, you had made a determination that you would tell the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I told the truth in May as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you told the truth each and every time that you made a statement to members of the Prosecution team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: In May I didn't remember things, and later on when I remembered, some things came to my mind and I said those, and I believe that there's nothing untrue that I said in May, with the exception of the word "Shala."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, certainly by June, then, when you've had a period of time to reflect, approximately a month, by that point in time any of the mistakes that you may have made as you sit here today, or you believe you may have made in May, had been remedied by June 17th; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you answer the question with regard to the guards were changed, you were asked the following question: "But in general, as a question, there was Zenel who checked people who came in for visits or whatever." Right? That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: What I said was that Zenel visited. Timi and Zenel visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that the translation here that I have, which is, "There has Zenel who checked people who came in for visits or whatever," is incorrect, and what you really were saying at that point in time was that Zenel was one of the number of people who visited the prison camp; right? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. Zenel was a soldier there, and what I said was that he visited from time to time the building we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, then, to be very plain, sir. Is it your testimony that Zenel was never a guard, and that is the position you took when you spoke with the Office of the Prosecutor some time ago in June, that he never was a guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know about the beginning, but for later on, I know that he wasn't a guard. It can be that he was a guard in the beginning, but he was frequently in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But with regard to Timi, I take it that Timi, he was a guard; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let's turn the page, sir, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's turn the page, sir, and you have a following answer which is: "And there was also Timi," which refers back to your initial statement that the guards were changed. Now, when you said there was also Timi, were you telling the truth then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what you were telling them was that Timi was a guard; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying this. He visited the place. I said it then and am repeating it now, that Timi and Zenel visited the place. I don't know about Zenel, whether he was a guard for a certain period of time, but they frequently visited this feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's information that you gave to the -- to the Prosecutors when you spoke to them in June, on June 17th, that Zenel and Timi were people who visited this place? Is that what you told them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, they visited them frequently. These visits were frequent ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you said that they visited frequently, I take it that you also informed them at that time what their duties were, and if I understand your testimony now, it is your position that you told the investigators on June 17th the duties of Zenel and Timi were those of soldiers as opposed to guards. You never indicated they were guards; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I never said they were guards. I didn't say this. I never said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All they did was visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: They visited the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if they visited the place and they had no relationship to the place, they had no duties with regard to the place; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know their duties. I know that they had duties because they visited the place frequently, but as I said, I don't know their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you certainly never would have said back in June 17th, after you'd had some time to reflect and remember who the guards were, that they had any duties as it related to the prison, would you? That's not something you would have said, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is how I said it. I don't know what the meaning is, but what I said was that they were regular visitors. I don't know what their task was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it's on -- I'm on page 44, and I don't know if the pagination now remains the same or not, sir, but you were asked the following question by Mr. Lehtinen: "Er, so were -- were Zenel and Timi persons that would stand at the gate of this prison?" And your answer was: "Timi and Zenel were people in charge there." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I'm not saying they didn't have responsibilities. They did have responsibilities because they went frequently to the place, but I didn't say that they were guards there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What about Agim Murrizi? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was he a guard there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the other person who you identified as being a guard there was a guy who had an injured foot; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is what I said in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. I'm now in June, sir. In June you said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever say in June, on June 17th, that this -- that an individual by the name of Shala had an injured foot, who might have had something to do with being a guard at the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't believe I've said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, once again, I'm not sure the pagination is going to be correct. I'm now on page 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's our page 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked a series of questions concerning who was standing at the gate at the time that you went up to the prison in order to do some business? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You say: "I think it was Agim." And then you go on to say: "Or that person who is now at the Tribunal, Shala, because he had an injured foot. It seems to me that it was him, Haradin. Because he had an injured foot, he stayed in the kitchen for a week to ten days." So there is no mistake here --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- in June it was your position and you told the Prosecutor that the possible guard at the prison with an injured foot was Shala, right, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it is written here, but I don't know if he had an injured foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you said it you knew he had an injured foot; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you decide that it was inconvenient for him to have an injured foot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: As I said in the beginning, I didn't remember things. I didn't remember things at all. I just spoke of things that I remembered. As persons, I can identify them very well, because I know both Shalas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's spend a little bit more time with your interview on the 17th. Now, on the 17th - I'm now on a -- I'm going to be on my page 61 - you took a break a little bit before the time of 1.14 when you had an off-the-record discussion. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you remember on June 17th speaking with Mr. Lehtinen off the record about some ostensible concerns you had with regard to security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I have don't know what page it is for you. Page 61 for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the bottom of page 59 and top of page 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: You're closing in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to you take a look at it. I suggest that what occurred, sir, was that you took a break, and during the break what you did was you began a negotiation process with Mr. Lehtinen concerning how your future was going to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't remember discussing the future. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, do you recall having a discussion with (redacted), and now we're back on the record since we don't know what was said off the record, in which (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, my goodness. I'm terribly sorry. I do apologise. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: We need to redact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We need to redact and then go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you told Mr. Lehtinen how many times you'd been to the prison, as it was called, in your June interview, when you told him that you'd been there two or three times in all, whether that was an accurate statement and an honest statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. But this is what I remembered. I didn't remember how many times I was. I couldn't tell you even now how many times exactly I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if you recall the other day when we were -- when we were chatting with each other, sir, one of the things we were discussing was how many off-the-record interviews you had with Mr. Lehtinen. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe I'm correct but please do correct me if I'm wrong, that one of the things you told us was that you talked to Mr. Lehtinen about certain facts, as we'll call them, off the record concerning your involvement with and experiences at Lapusnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I didn't speak off the record. Whatever I said, I said in the office in the presence of three individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We know that's not true because you've already admitted that what you did was you spent some time with Mr. Lehtinen in Lapusnik. You took a drive with him for a couple hours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. We travelled together, but we didn't discuss anything related to my experience in Lapusnik. I have already stated here I don't recall to have had any interpreters with us, and I don't think there was any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, in June, certainly by the time you've had your off-the-record discussion during the interview in which you've been given permission to change your answers, after that you certainly were in a position where discussions concerning Haradin Bala were accurate and truthful; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: In the second interview, I have told what was accurate with respect to Haradin Bala. In the second interview I said what I thought and believed and still do that was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so we're clear, in the second interview you identified Haradin Bala as having an injured leg; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you also said, and this will be page 93, I believe -- I'm sorry. Yes. You should start on page -- it's going to be page 91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Could you give Mr. Whiting some indication to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking for the best place. It says: "Yeah, okay. I want to speak a little bit about Haradin Bala." Let me you a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Preceding that: "And a Baretta pistol, okay, 7.65." Next: "Yeah, okay. Er -- then I want to speak a little bit about Haradin Bala." It would be the end of part 2 and the beginning of part 3 as it's been identified to me in the translation. I'll move to another -- I'll move to something else for the moment and we can come back to this. I won't forget it. I think from what I've heard, we're drifting further apart, not getting closer together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Do you have a page, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We do. The problem is that -- well, the problem is that your pagination started over again, and so the -- it's actually page 184.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You see it says: "I want to speak a little bit about Haradin Bala." And then you're asked: "When was the first time that you think you saw him?" "It must have been around the beginning of May or the beginning of June." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sorry. It's actually 185, that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why don't we give him 184, 185, and 186 to be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "But he the least of all stayed. He had an injured leg." You see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you said that in June, that certainly was the truth. By this point in time you certainly are telling the truth, are you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: But I don't remember now that he had an injured leg or foot. Maybe he had, but I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: When did you for the first time decide that he didn't have an injured leg? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I'm saying this because I don't remember that he had or didn't have an injured leg. He might have, but I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In May you said he had an injured leg. Earlier in this same interview you said he had an injured leg. Let me ask you this question: Would it be fair to say that the events were fresher in your mind then than they were last week when you testified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. No, they were -- my memory wasn't fresh at that moment. I didn't think about that. Even now I don't. I'm not interested in this. Once I leave this place, I will forget everything. I'm just saying what I think is accurate. He might have had an injured leg, but he wasn't lame. Someone else was lame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Another -- the other Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Ruzhdi. Ruzhdi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But what was his pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Karpuzi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That wasn't his pseudonym, sir. What was his pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I said Karpuzi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And his nickname was Shala; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you said with regard to this Shala: "He had an injured leg, and even if he did stay there, I don't think he beat people because he hated that sort of thing. He didn't like it." And then you're asked a question: "Okay. Did you see him in the fighting positions in Lapusnik?" And you said: "He was at the fighting positions, but when his leg was injured he went down there." And you were asked: "What kind of uniform did he wear?" And you answered: "I think he had a black waistcoat, but for the rest of it he wore civilian clothes." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't see it, but this is what I said. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this other Shala who you've identified as Ruzhdi Karpuzi, now that's a tall man; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He's big.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: -- tall. I say he might be 1.80 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you were asked -- and here's the next question you were asked with regard to the issue of the guard at the prison being Shala: "Okay. So do you think he was a guard in the prison?" And your answer is: "I don't think so, but he could have been because he had this injured leg."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's on page 187.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, your assistance, please. You maybe have to give him 188, too, just in case. Good. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, during this entire period this person that you're discussing here, this Shala you're discussing here, is Haradin Bala; right? That's what you're talking about. That's the subject matter here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but I think I said even earlier. I don't know if you understood me. I didn't want to speak about Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you didn't want to speak about Shala, I take it is it your testimony now that with regard to everything else but Shala you were telling the truth? Is that what you're telling us? That on May 28th and on June 17th the information that you gave to the Prosecution was the truth except for the information you gave about Haradin Bala? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: There were two Shalas and I wasn't so sure who was who. Maybe I was mistaken when I talked about them. I didn't -- didn't want to talk about them then or now. However, I know that what I said at the beginning and in the end was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, everything that we've discussed thus far, as far as you're concerned, is the truth; correct? Because these are things that you said, sir. You've had a chance to read them, to look at them, and to reflect upon them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I couldn't read them or look at them. But I'm saying that when it came to questions regarding Shalas, I might have confused them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall that after your interview on June 17th you went back the next day and had a further discussion with Mr. Lehtinen and others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall at that time you identified Shala?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You identified Shala as being 33 or 34 years old, tall, with a long face, dark, with an injured leg; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse -- I'm going to object. I think we should specify which Shala we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we're going to find out which Shala he's talking about because apparently he's confused, Your Honours, and I'm trying to make a determination to figure out if he knows who he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. He's not saying that he's confused. He's said he's not confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He said maybe at the time he was confused but not now. And I would submit that it's counsel that is trying to confuse matters here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, maybe you could rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Truly. But just for purposes he said, which is the reason that I took the position I took, his answer on page 25, line 17 was: "I couldn't read them or look at them, but I'm saying that when it came to questions regarding Shalas I might have confused them." Okay. Hopefully we have the same pagination. I'm on the June 18th interview, page 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We did it. And it's really quite serendipitous because you're asked the following question: "I have to take you back" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just wait a moment. It's being put before --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, surely. And you may have to give him 31, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, we'll give him both pages. A new problem. The version we have has only English on it. Do -- is that also --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'll move on and come back to it. I'm move on and come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I wouldn't have an objection to it just being read to him and the answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Okay. We'll dispense with the Albanian version for this question then. Please go ahead, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have to take you back to this Shala because to avoid mistakes in the future I just want to you describe him. His appearance? Yes. He was 33 or 34, tall, with a long face, dark, with an injured leg, and he lives in Shala. All the time until they took him to the position, to my position, he used to stay in the guest room there in Lapusnik, and he did some sort of job there. Okay. But do you think there could be any possibilities for the prisoners, for example, to have mixed between these two Shalas? And your answer, sir: "There is a -- there is a kind of congruence because the two did stay the same place, because Haradin was there for two weeks and because he [unintelligible] and this one stayed there about two months or so." Question: "Go ahead. Is it only because of the name or could -- could you mix them up because of their appearance?" Your answer, sir: "They do resemble each other rather well, but only this one has no moustache." Now, when you gave those answers discussing the Shalas, you were telling the truth then, weren't you? You had no failure of memory then, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. No. My memory hasn't left me even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would just note there was a compound question there, and the response I think is quite clear to the second part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Maybe you should put the first part again, Mr. Guy-Smith, for clarity.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Shalas, you were telling the truth then, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I have said the truth. Because one of them was younger. And he wasn't walking straight; he was walking rather lamely. And he didn't wear a moustache. The other one was older. He had a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall when you first told Mr. Lehtinen about your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't remember. Maybe on the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "maybe on the 18th of June," is that a memory that you have well fixed in your mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I know that after the interview immediately, either that day or on the next day, I submitted it. If I had mentioned it before, he would have asked me for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say you would have submit it had on that day, the day before, so we're clear now, June was hot; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. It was very hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How about October of that year? Do you recall October of that year? Was it hot then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in gaol.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You certainly wouldn't have given him your diary when you were in gaol, now, would you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. I handed over the diary with my own hand, and I was working out in the garden. It was very hot. That was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that you entered into your agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't remember. I was in gaol. It was by the end of September probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you entered into this agreement, at the same time a member of your family, without mentioning who that member was, was also in legal difficulty; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. He -- he was waiting for his case to be re-examined. It was being examined in the second degree court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This individual's case had not been completed, had it? As you say, waiting to be re-examined.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. No. It had been exhausted by the first instance court, but under the law you can take the case to the supreme or to the higher court, and he was waiting for the verdict or the ruling of that court. He was waiting for that ruling, which didn't come. We thought it would be a positive ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that was in what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I suppose we should go into private session for about a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you understand that in the event it is determined that you have lied that the agreement that you have with the Prosecution will no longer have any force and effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't care about that because I'm telling you, I have not lied. I have told the truth, then and now, with the exception of the fact that I have confused the names of Shalas. I know I am responsible to this Court if something turns out to be untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, my question, once again, is: Do you understand that if the Prosecution makes a determination that you've lied that your agreement is no longer in force and effect? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't understand that, but I'm telling you I don't care about that. I am responsible for what I'm telling you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, in all of these statements that you've made, did you ever tell anybody that Shala - and by this Shala I am referring to Haradin Bala - was present at a time when you were slapping women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know I've said this and that we were slapping. If someone has slapped someone else, it was me who questioned the person and not Shala or someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. You did admit to slapping a woman, and you said that at the time that Shala was behind you. Was that Shala 1 or Shala 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know who Shala number 1 and Shala number 2 are. Shala, who is from Shale village, he had other duties. But as to women, slapping women, there are two women concerned. I don't know what you mean. One of them I didn't slap. I just questioned her. The other I slapped once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The woman that you claim to have slapped once, you told us the other day that at the time that occurred that Shala was standing behind you. Was that the Shala who was from the village of Shale?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. He couldn't be there. When I slapped that woman, we were out in the field. As to the other woman that I questioned, that happened in the room of a house. I don't remember to have slapped her. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to any women that you have questioned or had contact with, is it your present testimony that Shala - and by that I mean the individual that you have identified as Shala - also known as Haradin Bala, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was not present? Is that your testimony? He was never present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: He was not present in the field in that case concerning two women, one of whom I slapped. In the second case, when we were inside, what was present was the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The guard that was present, is it your testimony that guard was not Shala? I'm suggesting to you that it was not Haradin Bala who was there. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I know that it was the guard who was present from the beginning and until the end. This is what I'm saying. But I don't know he was present at the moment that I interrogated that woman. I am not 100 per cent sure. I think he was, but I'm not 100 per cent sure. The guard was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: I think it would, Mr. Guy-Smith. And due to the redaction, as you know, we need to take a longer break than usual, which means that we will break now and reconvene at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to inform you that the prospects of having Judge Parker joining us today have dimmed considerably, so order will not be restored until tomorrow, I'm afraid. But in the meantime, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, apart from the interviews that we've discussed, you also made a statement which was the result of your contact with members of the Prosecution over a series of days in the months of -- in the months of December 2003, January 2004, and February 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know for how many days, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That took a considerable period of time, did it not? Without discussing how many specific days it was. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: It was within this period of time that you mentioned, two, three days maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But when you say two or three days, do you mean the entire process of your statement drafting took two or three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: It was each time for several hours a day. I don't know exactly how many days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall having a discussion with Mr. Mansfield sometime last week with regard to the number of days that it took for you to draft your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I remember that this was discussed, but I don't know how many days it took for the statement to be prepared, for things that been said to be repeated, for some photographs that I hadn't seen before. Mainly this was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the drafting process of this statement, during that period of time did you -- did you go through a review of your previous interviews with the Prosecution and make corrections to those matters that were to your then memory incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: The statement was discussed, but I don't think I had a statement, a previous statement like that one, like the one in May or June. I didn't have such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, were subject matters discussed in which it was pointed out to you that you had made mistakes with regard to certain facts that you had asserted were existing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I wasn't told that a mistake was made, but what was repeated at all times was that I have to speak the truth, the things that are entirely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, as you sit here today, it's true, is it not, that Haradin Bala came to Lapusnik right after May 9th? And by "right after" I mean within a couple of days after May 9th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, by the end of May. I don't know when exactly it was but the end may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you it was the beginning of May, right after the battle of May 9th, that Mr. Bala was present no later than the 11th or 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: It could be so, but I didn't see him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm also suggesting to you that he stayed, as you've indicated in the matter that we just discussed but a moment ago when you were making a distinguish -- any distinction between the congruent Shalas, that he stayed for approximately two weeks and then left Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The way the question is phrased, I think it's misstating the evidence. It's suggesting he has said that when that's simply not the case. I just think it's a confusing question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Can we have the basis, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Page 31: "There is a kind of congruence because the two did stay in the same place, because Haradin, er, was there for two weeks, and because he [unintelligble] and this one, referring to the other Shala, stayed there for about two months or so." That Shala being the one that he referred to on page 30, as 33 to 34, tall, with a long face, dark, and with an injured leg. He lives in Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I may, the reference there is to Lapusnik. It's to the kitchen in Gzim's compound. That's what he's talking about, not staying two weeks in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now we're into a matter of interpretation about what the reference is but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: I will sustain the objection, Mr. Guy-Smith, so if you want to pursue, you need to take another line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am suggesting to you, sir, that you did see Haradin Bala at Lapusnik. You saw him at the beginning of May, right after the battle of May 9th and that he stayed there for approximately two weeks, and thereafter you did not see him anymore. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, this is not the truth. I've never said this. What I've said is that one of the Shalas stayed there for about two weeks and took some administrative notes. The other Shala -- both Shalas remained in Lapusnik until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you gave your statement over a period of some days, at that time similar to the time that you've testified to here today, you once again were telling the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I was telling the truth even then. Even then I said that both of them remained in Lapusnik until the end. I didn't say that one of them left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to your general approach to the making of those statements, sir, because you've told us that in each statement that you've made you've told the truth, and once again I'm trying to make a determination with regard to the last statement, which is a statement that you signed, that during that process you were telling the truth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: As I said, with the exception that I mixed up the two Shalas, I have told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good. Now, with regard to the statement that you made -- you signed, when you made that statement, by that time your memory was quite good; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to your relationship to Haradin Bala, you were quite clear in your statement as to what precisely was your relationship with him, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: As I said, I was on good terms with everybody. As for Haradin, even at that time I thought that he wasn't a person who would cause -- or harm someone. And I am even of this opinion today. I have never seen him committing any harm to anyone, and I don't think he did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate -- I appreciate your opinion in that regard, but I'm asking you a slightly different question at this time, which deals with the fact that you told the Prosecutor in your statement - and I'm referring to paragraph 102, Mr. Younis - that you were good friends with Haradin; right? This is something we talked about last week.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what you said in your statement was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have the Albanian version and if it could just be put before the witness and him given an opportunity to look at it before the questions proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to take a look at paragraph 102?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that paragraph, you say a series of things. You've never heard anyone speaking a bad word about Haradin Bala. He was an obedient man, and I don't think he dared to disagree with any orders that were given to him. But I'd like to focus in on the next sentence because this is actually something we discussed last week. You said: "After the war I met Haradin a lot of times and we have become good friends."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I have met him after the war. We were friends during the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, my question, then: Is that information, the information that's contained in the statement that you signed, that being: "After the war I've met Haradin a lot of times," that's not true, is it? That's a false statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Not frequently. Frequently can refer to seeing him on a daily basis, weekly basis. I haven't seen him frequently. I might have met him two, three, four times maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Four times maximum. And then you go on to say: "And we have become good friends." Now, is that information, the information that's contained in the statement, that you have become good friends with Haradin Bala, that's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I said that we were friends during the war and after the war. There was nothing bad between us. Friends in Albanian, the word "miq," with refer to also in-law relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But that's not my question, sir. It says here: "We have become good friends." I take it that you have not become good friends with Haradin Bala having met him a maximum, as you put it, of four times after the war. You're not good friends with this man, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: We were all friends during the war and after the war. I don't know how you assess that, a good friend or a bad friend, but there was nothing bad going on between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I suggest to you that after the war you didn't meet Mr. Bala at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is what you think. I have met him during manifestations and social life in several places.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I further suggest to you, sir, that during the period of time that you saw Mr. Bala at Lapusnik at the beginning of May, you became aware of the fact that he had a heart problem. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that he had a problem, a heart problem, at that time. Maybe -- I don't remember. Maybe he had a problem, but I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you learned about Mr. Bala's heart problem as your friendship was budding after the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I could have learnt about his heart problem from others, but even from him. I've met also people whom I knew from Lapusnik and in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So as you sit here right now you can't tell us how you learned about Mr. Bala's heart condition nor when you learned about Mr. Bala's heart condition; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when I learned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the issue of the prison camp, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, with your assistance, page 241 of the statement. This would be June 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were having discussions with the members of the Prosecution, the subject matter of who was present at this prison camp when the prisoners were released came up; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you identified with some specificity who those individuals were, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. I don't know that even today. What I know is that 26 were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Apart from prisoners, you also identified with some specificity the guards who were present; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you identified them in the following manner, having been asked the following question: "Okay. Do you know who was actually in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prison camp when the prisoners were released?" And your answer was: "It was Ymer." He's dead; correct? You don't say that in here, but Ymer, that's Ymer Alushani, he's dead; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot read it at the moment, but yes, that's how it was. Now I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "In that he had taken the can and the ammunition and Zenel" -- we've talked about Zenel before. He was the individual who claimed to be part of the French Foreign Legion or the Foreign Legion; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I cannot find it here, but this is what I said. I didn't say that I took the cannon. It was Zenel that took the cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you also identified a third person being present in the prison camp when the prisoners were released, and that was Timi; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You say: "Those three were there." True?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This witness has this before him in English, and I would just ask that the -- rather than reading just little bits and pieces and then asking questions, if the whole passage -- because he then says that this is something he heard later in Klecka. But if it could be read to him and he could understand the full thing of what's being said before questions are put to him in bits and pieces. I don't think it's a fair way of proceeding without reading the whole passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I suggest you follow that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Okay. Do you know who was actually in the prison camp when the prisoners were released?" "It was -- it was Ymer and that he had taken the cannon and the ammunition, and Zenel and Timi. Those three were there." That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is what I heard, that they were there in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, to identify who those three individuals were, Ymer Alushani is an individual who we have had some discussion about. He's dead; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Zenel is the individual you identified as being part of the Foreign Legion. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Timi is a young man who also is dead; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you were then asked the following question by Mr. Lehtinen: "In -- in the prison camp?" And your answer is: "Yes." Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You then go -- you then get the following question and the following answer: "Okay. And where did you hear this from?" Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you answer: "A few days later they sent me to Klecka. I heard it from friends, soldiers." Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During your discussion with the members of the Prosecution, you did not mention at any time that either Shala, that being Haradin Bala or Ruzhdi Karpuzi, were present at the prison camp when the prisoners were released, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, maybe I didn't mention him. It is true that I didn't mention him. When they were released, I didn't see them. I didn't see Zenel or Timi. I didn't see any of them. I heard about this. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir, and what I am suggesting to you is the reason you didn't mention anyone with the name of Shala, whether it be Mr. Karpuzi or Mr. Bala, was because that was not information that you had. You were given quite specific information about who was present and that is the information that you conveyed to the Prosecution; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: As I said earlier, nobody gave me any information, and nobody even suggested that I should say anything. On the contrary. They said that I should tell the truth and only the truth and I abided to this, both for myself and others. If I needed to lie, I wouldn't have spoken about a part of my life, but because of the truth, I have told that then and I'm telling it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, sir, and what I'm saying to you is that on June 18th, when you were asked questions about the guards who were present, the information that you gave them, which you have just told us is the truth did not include Haradin Bala, did it? His name was not mentioned because that was a name that you did not have in your possession at that time as being present at the time the prisoners were released; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I had his name and disposition since 1998. I haven't mentioned it. I don't know why, but the fact is that I knew the name. Either they didn't ask about it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to whether or not you were asked or not, it's pretty clear that what we've been discussing here is a question that was asked of you as to who was actually present at the time the prisoners were released and your response; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And this is what I heard, not what I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, sir. What I'm getting to is that in your response you identified specific individuals. You identified a place. You identify that you had heard the information, and did you not in any fashion whatsoever indicate that Haradin Bala was part of that particular cabbala, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I didn't say that I didn't hear that he was part of it. Maybe what I've heard is that the prisoners were released and that Haradin Bala had no more tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Clearly that's something you would have said on June 18th if that's something you'd heard, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: If they had asked me about it, I would have told them that, on the 18th of June and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the failure then for any mention of Haradin Bala's name is because you weren't asked. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. This is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Witness, I represent Isak Musliu. Do you agree that you are a liar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Not at all. You have to prove it before you tell someone you are a liar. It seems to me this -- the use of this word in English sounds to me like a wise saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree you're a hypocrite?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I have no words to say to that. I've never thought of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you someone who would do and say anything to save yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Absolutely no. No, I don't care at all about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you someone who will do and say anything to improve your own position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I don't improve my position with the past. I acknowledge what I've done, and I claim responsibility for that. Whoever may raise indictments against me for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree that you are a coward, a moral coward?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Not at all. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree you are someone who pretends to build up your own importance at the cost of the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Had I done that, I would have said that I have not lied to any -- I have not beaten anyone, I have not seen anyone. And this is what I have said -- would I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree that you are a jealous, envious opportunist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Not at all. I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree you are a sadistic bully? You're smiling.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. No, that I don't believe at all. No. I a sadistic bully? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you a member of a rogue element within the KLA, a bunch of undisciplined thugs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. No. The KLA was well organised, and I stood by it until the end. Mistakes were made. As the case with is everything, you may not like something, but what you are putting to me is not true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree you've benefited from being a witness for the Prosecutor in this trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: On the contrary. I have been a loser. I don't think anyone in my position would claim to have benefited anything from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could we please go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree that you were a smuggler and profiteer before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Not during the war. I didn't have time to do that. If I had, I would have smuggled in any kind of weapons if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Before the war, do you agree that you were a smuggler and a profiteer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: If the law prescribes for certain weapons as being such, that is 10 or 12 weapons I have, most of them I have kept for myself, but the others I have sold to my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could the witness please have in front of him the Albanian version of his statement to the OTP, dated the -- or the long statement, the one taken in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Witness, you're going to need to have that statement in front of you for all of my questions so don't part with it if you'd be so kind. You're also going to need to have other documents as well. In light of the answers to the questions I've just asked, I want you to look, please, at paragraphs 9, 10, and 11 of that statement that you signed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the interpreters, I'm going to both take this slowly and I'm going to paraphrase paragraphs 9, 10 and 11. If I miss anything out that's important, Mr. Whiting will deal with it later. Paragraph 9 deals with a period from 1983 to 1986, I suggest, if you read the totality of your statement, and it says: "During the next few years, I travelled in Europe buying and selling goods and doing occasional jobs. I travelled between Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary and Italy, coming back to Kosova every two to three months." First question: What goods are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: These were all goods that were permissible to be traded under the law. Various goods. The Romanian government was interested, and the Turkish government, and many Eastern countries were interested in such goods, boots, Adidas boots, watches, trousers, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were they stolen goods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. No. They were purchased in one country. For example, in Turkey, they were not original goods, and they were sold. We had to leave. I didn't have a job, so I had to live on something, and this was a way, a possible way for me to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The statement goes on. "From 1986 onwards, I dealt with cars. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. This was not an official business but just my way of making a living for my family." Were these stolen cars that you were trading in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. Absolutely no. They had to be sold. If one of them was identified as such, that is as stolen, you might end up in gaol. So I took care not to engage in stolen cars trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: From 1990 onwards, it goes on, it says: "I was involved in illegal import of weapons to Kosovo together with my good friend Ymer Alushani." It goes on in the paragraph as follows: "The business was risky, and I only sold weapons to persons that I trusted and whom I knew wouldn't talk and boast about it." Have you read that yourself there in that statement, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it true what you say there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: It's not true with respect to the import. To import something means to bring some good from one country to another. But it is true that I purchased them and that I sold some of them. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And is it true when you say you only sold these illegally imported weapons to persons that you trusted? Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you absolutely sure about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: None of the weapons I sold to people, none of them was sought by the law. All of them were used in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If you listen to me carefully, there's a fair chance you'll leave that witness box sooner rather than later. Is it true when you told the Prosecutor in a signed statement that you "only sold weapons to persons that I trusted"? Was that the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, then, could you explain why, please, on the 15th of March of this year, day 51 of this trial, you sat in that chair and told this Tribunal that only part of them that you sold were to people you trusted? Was it only some of them or was it all of them? Which is the truth, what you said here on oath or what you said in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could I please have a page reference for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's the unperfected version. It's day day 51, it's page 7, line 5. "Part of them I sold to people I trusted."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I apologise to Mr. Whiting. All of my references from transcripts, I'm afraid, are the unrevised ones. I apologise. I'm not trusted with the revised ones for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have the unrevised ones as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, you're not trusted either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now which is the truth: All or just part were sold to friends you trusted, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I think I already stated a large part of the weapons I did not sell. I kept them at home. Another part, smaller part, I sold, and what I sold, I sold to people whom I trusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You agree you were, before the war, a gunrunner. This was an illegal import of weapons into Kosovo for profit, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: The Serbian army distributed weapons to the Serbs. So it was the wish of each and every Albanian to possess a weapon, even though it was considered a criminal offence if it was found that an Albanian was engaged in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you donate the funds you made to the KLA, or did you put them in your pocket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: There were no funds. I may say that usually I sold a weapon at the same price I bought it. Maybe sometimes for 100 Marks more, Deutschmarks. I only wanted to provide weapons to the people who wanted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And when you made a profit of 100 Marks or more, what did you do with the profit? Did you put it in your pocket or did you give it to the KLA, which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I -- of course I put it in my own pocket, and I didn't give it to anyone. I used it for something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You're not a hypocrite?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't get what you are wanting to tell me. When it was a question -- when I was dealing with guns, I didn't know about the existence of the KLA. What I had to pay to the Kosovo provisional government I did so regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions last week about your involvement in the world of drugs. You recollect being asked a large number of questions concerning that, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were at pains to tell us on a number of occasions that you were not a drug dealer. You were somebody who simply mediated between the buyer and the seller. That's your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. I've told you what was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I suggested to you a little earlier that you perhaps were part of a renegade group within the KLA. I want you to turn -- and you denied it. I want you to turn, please, to paragraph 49 of the statement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be far easier for Your Honours to follow this part and other parts of my cross-examination were you to have the statement. I think Mr. Khan is happy with that and so is Mr. Guy-Smith. Would it assist Your Honours to have a copy of the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: If you're going to dwell on this at some length, certainly it would be of assistance. So we would be happy to read whatever you want to put in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I hope I won't dwell and I hope it won't be at excessive length but I need to put some of it. Are there copies available? No, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: It's your part now so you should have provided us with it if you wanted to do it, but we don't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'll read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This is -- this is paragraph 49 under the heading "Start of the war." "In the spring of 1998, I became part of Ymer Alushani's group of fighters called Zjarri, meaning fire. This group did some sporadic operations against Serb interests, but mostly it was a matter of being prepared for the war. I didn't call myself a KLA soldier even if I was preparing for war ... I felt that I became a member of the KLA when I joined this group, but for the above-mentioned reason I didn't admit it..." And in paragraph 50, you tell the Prosecutor in your statement that the group consisted of friends of Ymer's, that you arranged for some more rare arms that were hard to get, and the group in Likovc had a general plan for organising the army, but Ymer would have formed this group with or without their permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: First of all, could I interrupt myself and hand up to the Court -- the Tribunal, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This Zjarri unit was no part of the KLA, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This was until 10 or 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's just look at what you told this Tribunal last week about the work of this group. Day 51, for Mr. Whiting's benefit, page 26 of the unrevised transcript. "In addition to getting prepared," you told us last week, Witness, "sometimes we also used to escort somebody. On one occasion I escorted somebody to Orahovac. There was nothing major that we did." Do you remember telling us that on oath last week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I didn't say so. I didn't escort myself. I said that we escorted up to Orahovac. If I have said "we have escorted," I didn't mean myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You know what's coming, don't you? Because Mr. Whiting then asks you what you meant by the word "escort." Do you remember what you told him last week from that chair that the word "escort" meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: It means to accompany somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's a lie. That's a downright, deliberate, blatant, barefaced lie, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: You said that you yourself have escorted. My point is that I have never myself been involved in the escort of -- alone. We have been three persons that went to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Question from Mr. Whiting: "What do you mean you tried to escort him?" Your answer on oath on a transcript. Listen to me: "We followed him. I mean, we follow him. We wanted to kill him." "Escort" means assassinate, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: The entire escort operation had the intention of killing. You might use whatever word you like, escort or whatever, but our goal was to kill that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Please be good enough, Witness, not to put words in my mouth. You were the one who came up with the word "escort," and when Mr. Whiting perfectly properly pressed you as to what it meant, you told us last week that it was meaning to kill.
