On one occasion you said, "We went to someone, told him not to hang around with Serbs or Serbian secret service people, these kinds of things." You were a hit squad, weren't you? You were a sadistic bully during this part of the war, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: That's not true. We told this person not to mix up, not to meddle with the Serbs, that's true, but not in the sense that you are putting to me as a sadistic bully. This I don't accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you not deny that you tried to kill him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, I don't deny that. This is what we were after, killing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Quite. Let's just before I go in to ask you a number of different questions regarding different parts of the evidence that you've given us over the last five and a half days, I want to ask -- see if you and I can agree some sort of chronology of important dates. I'll use a neutral term. (redacted), a member of your family was alleged to have been involved in drug supplying. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is what was claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: (redacted), these defendants made their first appearances before this Tribunal in The Hague. Do you recollect seeing that on television and reading about it in newspapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We'll come back to an aspect of that a little later on. On the 27th of May, 2003, as we've been hearing at some length over the last few days, you were interviewed by the investigators for the OTP, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just out of an abundance of caution, could we redact the date which appears at page 54, line 23? It could -- it could identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: That should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Forgive me. It's sometimes difficult to appreciate what might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: It was a close call.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hope I will err on the side of caution in this regard for the rest of the time on my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We got to the 27th of May, 2003, and your lengthy interview. 17th and 18th of June of 2003, you were of course interviewed at even greater length, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, so just under one month later, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And we better go into private session for this, I think, for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Would I be right in suggesting that your cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor and investigators, your statements, your interviews, indeed your evidence here all came about because you could see a way of avoiding prosecution for your own crimes during the war? Would I be right in suggesting that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: My crimes committed during the war? That was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't think so. This was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at some of your crimes later. Was your cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor and investigators, your statements, your interviews, indeed your evidence here all come about because you could see a way of avoiding gaol for drug dealing, for possession of firearms and a hand grenade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: That's not true. I possessed arms even before the war, when it was considered even more dangerous and you might face a greater sentence. I didn't care, and I still possessed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to move on now to deal with various aspects of your evidence as I indicated that I would, and I'm going to take the headings from the same headings that appear - not all of them - in your witness statement, and I'm going to start with one or two questions regarding your diary. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the purpose of this diary. This was secret, was it, between you and the pieces of paper you were writing on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Every diary is a secret document. It's meant to be kept for yourself, and this is what I did. I knew I had it in me. I didn't mention it at all because I believed it was my personal property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you in any way, in any sense reluctant to hand this diary over to investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I was reluctant. I didn't want to give it over, but when they asked me, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This wasn't for publication, this diary. Indeed, it wasn't for the sight of anyone else in the world. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Every diary is for oneself. This is what I consider mine there were other parts in it which I had to fill in. It was only a beginning. I had put down some notes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Please be good enough to answer my question. It wasn't for the sight of anyone else in the world. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. And I had never shown it to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Therefore, it was a place, this diary, a document that could contain your deepest, darkest secrets, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I said that I had -- it contained my impressions and notes about some days of the war and nothing about the post-wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to understand, Witness. Is it your evidence regarding this diary that when one reads it one could anticipate that somewhere it would contain everything that happened to you that was important and of significance? Is that the position regarding this diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, some things which were of importance to me. These were the things that I wrote about, but in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We'll come back to what is not there later. I want to move on to another heading I'm stealing from your statement, and that is "Location." Are you aware that Ruzhdi Karpuzi has given evidence before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that, but I didn't see it with my own eyes. I read about it in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You allege in your statement to the investigators, your long statement, that in paragraph 30, Ruzhdi Karpuzi from Sedlare was responsible for keeping records and collecting and filing statements made by the prisoners. Paragraph 30. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you aware that on his oath Ruzhdi Karpuzi has denied emphatically that allegation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that he has, and bearing in mind that he has, it follows, therefore, that one of you isn't telling the truth about this. That follows, doesn't it? Are you the liar or is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is what it turns out to be, but he is responsible for what he has testified here. I am responsible for mine. If what he said comes to be true, then I will be responsible for what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's move on, please, to another paragraph under the heading of "Location" in your statement. Paragraph 47. "I will later describe all the occasions when I visited this compound," and that's what you're talking about, the compound, "where prisoners were held. I didn't go there a lot of times because I hated the fact that people were kept in those circumstances, and I didn't want to be seen there." Do you see that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is that paragraph true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you're not a hypocrite?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If you hated it so much, why did you keep going back and mistreating people who were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I hated it because many people were taken there on basis of speculation, without any ground, evidence, and that violence was used against them. That's why I hated the place. I had to go because I had to, but not to maltreat or mistreat someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So you are someone who deeply believes in the principles of justice, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I am not acquainted with laws or with conventions, but I do know the human laws. I know what is good and what is bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you're not a hypocrite?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: You might say so, but I'm telling you that I know not the laws but know only what is human and inhuman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Why didn't you confide in your diary your hatred of this place and the way that other human beings were being treated if it be true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I couldn't get hold of other notes which certainly must exist somewhere. I told you, I didn't play much importance to that -- didn't pay much importance to that diary thinking that I would come back to it another time when I had more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No. What you didn't pay much importance to was the maltreatment you were dishing out to people in that place as part of this renegade group that you were a proud member of. That's what wasn't important to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Of course. This was the title that Serbia gave us, terrorists and renegades. I was not a renegade. I didn't maltreat anyone. If I did so, I'm certain that that person or those persons would one day come to this court and testify against me. With respect to what you are saying about protection, I am telling you that I want that protection to be lifted. I don't want protection from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, you're going to get protection from me and from this Tribunal, so you can't play that game with us. I want to be clear: Is it your evidence on your oath that you did not maltreat anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I'm not saying -- I am saying that I didn't maltreat anyone with the exception of a slap I might have given to someone, and this I don't see. I don't consider this as a maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We'll come back to things you did. I want to ask you about a document you were asked to look at some time ago now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I wonder if through the usher the witness could be provided with the bundle of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And I want you to go, please, to tab 14. Of this document. It's tab 14, the travel permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Maybe we could get the exhibit number from Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: 171. I know if I dally long enough, Mr. Younis will help. Thank you. 171, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. May I ask when Your Honour is thinking of taking a break so I can keep an eye on the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: I think another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, this is what has been called a travel permit. And I just want to remind you at day 51, page 73 of the unrevised transcript, what you said about this document, so would you please be good enough to listen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "Do you recognise that document?" And your reply was: "Yes, I do. This was how these travel permits were organised or issued. This is how they were formulated. I think this is a little bit longer than what I used -- was used to, but this is more or less it." Question from Mr. Whiting: "And you would use these travel permits during June and July of 1998?" Answer: "Yes. It was not possible to leave the position without having permission to leave it." Question: "And on this, this example, it's signed by a commander. In Lapusnik, would it be signed by Qerqiz?" And in answer to that leading question you said: "Yes, Qerqizi." Now, did you provide this travel permit to the investigators, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. No, I just saw that travel permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I wonder if you would be good enough to look at the original, U0023034, that's in Albanian, and I'd like you to put it alongside the typed copy. There's a rather important thing missing, I suggest. After the word "Celiku" in the typed version is simply a closed quotation mark, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In the original, it's V, a Roman V, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This travel permit, if that's what it is, seems to have come out of a unit called Celiku V therefore. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but what I said was that that travel document resembled this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I know you did. Where was Celiku V during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it was somewhere in Lladrovc or Terpeze. I don't know where their base was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Who was its commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: What about the person who signed this travel permit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I know this person as a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put those away. We're dealing with this part of your statement in evidence that relates to the start of the war. I want to ask you this: When you were in Lapusnik, did you have a beard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: When you went to the Llap zone later on in 1998, did you have a beard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: For some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And by the way, did you ever tell anyone in the world that you were a commander in the Llap zone during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Think very, very carefully before you answer that question. Did you ever tell anyone in the world that you were a commander in the Llap zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I said no, because my profession was that of to be a commander of my own self there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let's leave philosophy to one side, shall we. You never were a commander of anything or anyone, were you, during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: As I said, profession is something else. With my profession, I couldn't be someone's commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So if you have ever told anyone that you were a commander in the Llap zone, that would be a lie, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to move on to another aspect of your evidence still under the same general heading and that is discipline of soldiers. You gave us an account last week of the sending home of another soldier. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And do you remember telling us why it was that this man was, according to you, dismissed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I have told you that. Because of drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's simply not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is very true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He was sent home because he was terribly sick, ill. Nothing to do with beer at all, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: He stayed there for another ten days or two weeks waiting for his weapon to be returned. If he was sick, he would have gone to see a doctor or to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He was so sick he was sent from Lapusnik not because of beer drinking. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to move on to something else. You have told us that you were never disarmed. Was that the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Again, Witness, I urge you to be careful and take your time. Are you saying you were never disarmed during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Never. There were intentions to do so, but I was never disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that not only were you disarmed but you were disarmed by Qerqiz, and I'm going to suggest to you that you were disarmed by Qerqiz for a very specific reason. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And what's more I'm going to tell you when it happened. It happened somewhere in the last week of May of 1998. But you deny that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It is true, because you were disarmed, I suggest, because it was discovered that you were going to leave Lapusnik to go and murder somebody. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, this is not true. I didn't go anywhere without an order. Even if I went to kill someone, I did it with an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I suggest to that this was outwith, outside your orders, that this was you acting as I suggested you are a sadistic bully and in this case worse, a man who was prepared to murder. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I agree as for the fact that I joined the war not to greet them, but I went there to kill. And there was no chance that I was able to leave the position in May from 4.00 in the morning till 9.00 in the afternoon. We sometimes stayed there even without having any food at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need to for same reasons as before to have a longer break, 30 minutes, so we reconvene at ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sometime, I suggest, Witness, between the 19th and the 25th of May, 1998, Qerqizi, Isak Musliu, disarmed you, took your weapon away from you. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. With the exception of the fact that he wanted to have one of my revolvers and I gave it to him through Ymer voluntarily. We exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have suggested to you, Witness, and I will not name the name, that you were dismissed by Qerqizi when it was discovered that you were intending to leave Lapusnik not to go and get a weapon, as you told him, but to murder a named individual, and you have emphatically denied that suggestion. Furthermore, I'm going to suggest to you that you were disarmed, and you were sent away, and indeed the fact is, the truth is that Qerqizi himself did not see you again in Lapusnik. You disagree with that, don't you? You say you stayed in Lapusnik until it fell in July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is very much true and nobody can deny it. It is the way I'm saying it here. I was never disarmed, and I was there till the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on, please. I want to deal briefly with Agim Zogaj, otherwise known as Murrizi. Do you follow? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You told us before this afternoon that you did not watch on television the appearance of accused here in The Hague in February 2003, but you became aware of the fact that accused men were appearing here in this case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I didn't say I didn't see him on television. I said that I didn't see someone else when you asked about Shala. As for this person, I'm sure that he appeared on TV for several days and that I've seen him and that I've recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's very interesting. You recognised the man on TV, did you, as the man Murrizi that you recognised from the camp in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Of course I knew him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, answer my question. You recognised on TV, did you, the man known as Murrizi from the camp in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: He wasn't on TV. On TV, there was another person, and I have recognised the second person as well because I have reasons to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The person you are no doubt talking about was a man called Agim Murtezi, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Agim Murtezi was an innocent man, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: He was for some time a policeman for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Please answer my questions. I'm sure you understand them. Agim Murtezi, for the purposes of this case, was an innocent man, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Agim Murtezi was innocent. He was not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He was not the man known as Murrizi at the camp, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. I knew it very well, from the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you pick up a telephone and tell anyone they'd got the wrong man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. That didn't interest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Justice doesn't interest you. I thought a little while ago this afternoon you said that justice did interest you. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Justice does interest me. But there are people who are paid for those things, people who should lead justice, and that's why there was no need for me to say anything about this. If I were asked, then I would say that that was the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Witness, does it mean from that answer you would have stayed silent and watched this innocent man get convicted of crimes he did not commit because you weren't interested? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not paid for that. There are people who are paid for that and who will identify him as an innocent. I wasn't asked. If I were asked, I would have said that I know that person, he was a policeman in the service of Serbia, and that he was never in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You're not a moral coward?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I am not a moral coward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's move on, please, to some questions regarding the prison as you've described it. This prison and what went on there, according to you more than once in evidence before this Tribunal, really wasn't something of particular interest to you. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On the evidence you've given us, do you also agree that you seem to be saying clearly that Qerqizi was at the heart of the operation of this prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No. Qerqiz was the commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it your evidence, is it your view of all of this that Qerqizi was in some way responsible for what went on, including other things, things also at this so-called prison? Is that your view of Qerqizi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: My opinion about him is that he was a commander, but I'm not saying that he was in charge of the prison or that he had any responsibilities but that he was a commander above the soldiers there, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree it might be perfectly possible for Qerqizi simply to have been fighting the war and have nothing whatever to do with this so-called prison? Might that be the case, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: He always participated in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now answer my question, which was: Is it perfectly possible for Qerqizi simply to have been fighting the war and have had nothing to do with this so-called prison? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In the light of that answer, I press on. I want to ask you, please, how many times do you say that you were in the compound where there was a prison between May the 9th and July the 25th when Lapusnik fell? How many times were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Between 9th of May and 26th of July, it is possible that I've been there six or seven times. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Has that always been the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I know that I've been there two or three times on duty, but later on I remembered that I've been there several times as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Have you ever on another occasion denied being there at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Again, I urge caution. Think carefully before answering. Have you ever on a previous occasion to anyone denied ever being there at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't remember that. You should identify the persons who I have told this, if I have told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, his name's Lehtinen amongst others. And I'm going to show you your interview, please, in Albanian, of the 27th of May, 2003, and I'd like you to go to page 11 of the Albanian version, if you'd be good enough. I think you have it there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the English page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The English, page 12. Your Honours, I think the witness has -- does he have the interview there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: We'll find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe he has the statement. I don't think he still has the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith had the interview before him on a number of occasions. I wonder if -- Mr. Younis's help as always. Could the whole interview go before the witness. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Witness, this is your interview with the investigators transcribed in July but in fact having taken place on the 27th of May of 2003, and I want you to go to page 11 of your version. It's the bottom of page 12 of our version in English. Now, the passage I'm looking for, Witness, is this: It is AW, who begins with the words "Let's go back to this, when this started to be used by the KLA, this compound." Would you be good enough, please, to find the question that begins in that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: For Mr. Whiting's benefit, near the bottom of page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And would you please indicate when you've found it. "AW: Let's go back to this, when this started to be used by the KLA, this compound."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: It's not on page 11 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Would Your Honours bear with me while I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I can just be of some assistance. On the Albanian it doesn't appear as AW. Because the questions are being put by the interpreters, so the interpreter's initials are identified. So that may be the source of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's go back to this. DB. I beg your pardon. Thank you, Mr. Whiting. DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It's about a dozen lines up from the bottom of page 11, Witness. "kur, kur," it starts. Do you have that? Page 11, count 13 lines up from the bottom and you'll have it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Would you follow this with me in your language, please. Oh, by the way, do you speak English? Just answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you speak English well enough to conduct this cross-examination without the benefit of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I understand it almost 100 per cent, but I have difficulties in speaking it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: "Let's go back to this," says the questioner. "When this started to be used by the KLA, this compound, when it started to be used was used by soldiers to watch television. It was also used -- there were certain rooms that were used to keep prisoners that were being held by the KLA; isn't that correct?" And here follows your answer: "I was not somebody who they would much trust, because being an LDK member, I was not somebody who would be taken in trust in Lapusnik as far as Lapusnik is concerned. I was basically busy with organising and setting up things in these bunkers." "Okay," says Mr. Lehtinen. Reading on: "And the second reason me being a person not trustworthy was I had Serb friends." The question: "I understand, but you knew that the KLA was using it to hold prisoners. Everybody knew that," said the questioner. You reply: "I heard it that way. I've heard it, the same thing, but I haven't witnessed it for myself. I haven't seen it for myself." That is a massive lie, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: That's what is written here, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And it's a lie, isn't it, a deliberate lie to the investigator? You are denying ever going there, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't understand whether the question was from May, because I didn't know of it in May. But if it is the way it is here, that's the way the lie is then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is that your best answer to this point, Witness? Is that all you want to say about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: What I said is that if the question was have I ever seen it and this is the question, then it's a lie. But if it's -- the question concerns May, then the truth is that I didn't see it in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The Tribunal will decide what the words of the question mean. I put to you at the beginning of my cross-examination that you were a liar and you did not agree with me. Do you want to change your mind about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: In this case, I don't want to change anything. This is true. I either didn't think of it or wasn't prepared to give a statement at all. Maybe I just wanted to be over and done with on that day and go home, if we're talking about the May statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You wanted it over and done with and go home. That was your approach, was it, to your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on the 27th of May, 2003? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't go there for several days, and when I went, I wanted to finish with that as soon as possible and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In any event, the case is, is it not, that whether you were under suspicion by any of your comrades or whether you were not trusted at all, on your own account you ignored restricted access and made a number of visits to this place where people were being held? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: It's not they didn't trust me. Maybe there was some who didn't trust, but those who knew me, they trusted me. In a way, everybody coming from outside and who were not able to face those tortures by the Serbian government, they were even greater patriots. Serbs were my neighbours, and I had nothing bad with them, with the exception of Milosevic's regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you confide in your private and personal diary that you were going to this place that was a prison where people were being held against their will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I'm saying even now that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Of course that presumably is in those parts of the diary hidden in a bottle somewhere in the mountains in Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: They have nothing to do with that. Even the diary has nothing to do with them. I'm saying I'm telling you the truth, and if you prove the opposite, then you can find out who is a liar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The advantage of this system, you see, Witness, is I have to prove nothing. I am asking you whether there exists anywhere in the world a single piece of paper - diary, notebook, or whatever you want to call it - that contains any reference at all to this prison and these prisoners. Does it exist? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, you do, because you would have written it. Now, answer my question. Does it exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. The witness answered the question and now the counsel is arguing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I will allow that. Please continue, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Please be good enough, on His Honour's direction, to answer the question I have asked you. You have said you wouldn't know. I'm asking you whether or not any piece of paper exists anywhere in the world with you writing to you yourself, your diary, regarding this prison. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I'm not certain, I said. I haven't seen yet some of its -- of these parts since 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were, weren't you, a skilful interrogator of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: The ones I have interrogated, it was in the month of February. It's not true that I interrogated them. I have already identified whom I have questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let's go into private session and talk about one person in particular.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction. It was not February, it was in brief. It's the same word in Albanian. Correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm asking you about a particular named individual, and I remind you please we're in open session. You have indicated that he had spread rumours and that he seemed very arrogant to you. Is he the same man whose head you lifted with the barrel of a gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Was that somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You're not a sadistic thug?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: If you call me this because I lifted -- I raised his head with the butt of my rifle, then I am. But as far as I know about a sadistic person, this is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let me go on to some -- another subject in which I suggest you did act sadistically, viciously, and spitefully. Let's talk about a Serb female. You remember telling us about her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you ashamed of what you did as far as this woman is concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I didn't do anything to her. I released her. When the order was given, I released her and I accompanied her up to her place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I repeat: Are you ashamed of what you did as far as this woman is concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I don't know that I did something wrong to her. If I did something wrong to her, she should have testified -- testified against me. Anyone would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Oh, I see. If they don't come and testify against you, then your position is that you've done nothing wrong. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I have done nothing wrong to that female. I questioned her, and then after a day I released her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what you did to this woman to whom you did nothing wrong. First of all, you gave her a lift in your car from Fustica to Lapusnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Day 54 for Mr. Whiting if he wishes to follow it, page 6 of the transcript. "She pretended she was handicapped."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: How did she pretend she was handicapped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: She feigned to be mentally sick. That's what she claimed. And there were some signs that show that she suffered from some mental illness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: She had things in her baggage, you told us, which only people who have mental disabilities could carry. What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Is it to identify persons suffering from mental difficulties. Some words she said, some things she kept in her bag. The amulets she kept in her bag. These showed to me that she was suffering from some mental disabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So rather than take pity on her, you took her back to a place, and you and your mates beat her on the feet. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Instead of taking pity on her, I took her to the place because she had surrendered to me. And if I let her go, I would have to be -- I would be held accountable for that. So that's why I took her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You beat her on her feet, didn't you, you and your comrades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Maybe someone has beaten her for as long as she stayed there, but during the time she stayed with me, nobody beat her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Would you have the common decency, please, to tell this Tribunal the truth. In a signed statement to the investigators, you said, "We beat her on the feet." Now, please, would you please tell us and admit what you did. You beat her, didn't you, you and your friends, on the feet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: "We" is plural, but it doesn't show that I was there with my comrades. I was there alone and the guard was present, but if others beat her they would be described as comrades also, but I didn't beat her. I don't remember to have given a slap or to have beaten this woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you try to stop this thing happening to her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I just handed her over, and on the next day I released her. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: But why if you didn't see it did you put in a statement that you signed as being the truth that you did? "We beat her on the feet." The words are very simple. They mean what they say, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the statement is still before the witness. If he could just be -- if his attention could be drawn to the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting is quite right. In the interests of the economy of time, I'm not being fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Paragraph 131 of your own witness statement, please. Would you go to that. Paragraph 131. And tell me when you've found it. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: "I took her to the prison in Lapusnik," you say. I'm summarising. "I recall for sure I took her into the room downstairs. Had her sitting in a corner inside the door. I checked her belongings and questioned her. I think I was accompanied by someone, but I cannot remember who. The woman acted mad, and on other hand kept trying to convince us she was a Muslim. We didn't get anything out of her. We hit her a few times on the soles of her feet with a wooden stick, but it didn't seem to have any effect." Is that statement true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: It must be true, but I don't remember myself beating her. I know that others beat her and she said so, that someone had beaten her on the soles of her feet, but I don't -- I didn't see any injuries on her or anything. I only saw that she was very upset, but that was it. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Would you like to apologise to her now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, yes. I would like to apologise to anyone for anything I have done, for any mistakes I made. At a later time I've asked someone whom I beat, I apologised to him, and after that we became good friends. He -- he forgive me -- he forgave me, sorry, and then after that we became good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This is of course the same woman you tied to a tree and told her you would shoot her if she deviated from the path on her being released, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you tie her to a tree with rope, string, a belt, wire, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: With a string. I had -- I had string with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's move on, please, to deal with another topic, and for this it involves a named and identifiable individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I ask to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'll be careful not to mention the name. I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 167 dealing with part of this incident, Witness, you say that you were asked to participate in his murder, but you refused to do so, and I quote you: "I don't kill Albanians," is what you report yourself as saying. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I've always said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You don't kill Albanians, you just terrify and torture them instead. Isn't that the position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: This is what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You are, I suggest, or you were part of a renegade group of thugs who did just that, and you're seeking wickedly to draw in people such as Qerqizi into this fabricated story. That is what I suggest you are doing. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64
utterances.text: No, not at all. A member of a renegade group, as you are saying, I was there only for some 20 days during the NATO airstrikes, but I wasn't connected to any command. Otherwise, I was under the command of what you know. For that period, you could say I was in that renegade group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, would that be a convenient moment? And I'm asked may I recover back from Your Honours the witness statement so I have no need for you -- the witness statement made by this witness? Thank you. There's no application to exhibit them, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: You can have it with our scribbles on it for whatever use you may find for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, they will go no further. I'm sorry I could not finish this evening. I apologise. But Your Honours, I understand that given the schedule tomorrow, that's not going to interfere with the timetable. I will finish well within time tomorrow. Mr. Whiting I know will be re-examining. We have one other witness that will take possibly less than the day tomorrow. So we're not running behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. No fault of yours. We have now reached the end of the hearing today so we must adjourn. We will reconvene tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 31st day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
